We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u=1+{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{1+0}-\frac{1}{1+{a}^{2}}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-\frac{1}{1+{a}^{2}}) \\  & =-1+0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the total area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve $y=\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}$ and the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x
$$

We start by calculating the first of these integrals:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x
$$

We calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u={x}^{2}$, then $\text{d}u=2x\,\text{d}x.$ Hence, the antiderivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{u}{2}))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x & =-{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{x}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }{(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}))|}_{a}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(0)-\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{{a}^{2}}{2})) \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}(0-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x=\frac{\pi }{8}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{|x|}{{x}^{4}+4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}+\frac{\pi }{8} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the curve and the $x$-axis by calculating the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{e}^{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}3{e}^{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{x+2}{|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =3{lim}_{a\to -\infty }({e}^{0+2}-{e}^{a+2}) \\  & =3({e}^{2}-0) \\  & =3{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand $3{e}^{-|x|+2}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x=3{e}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }3{e}^{-|x|+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{e}^{2}+3{e}^{2} \\  & =6{e}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{e}^{-3|x|+2}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{-3|x|+2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-3|x|+2}\,\text{d}x
$$

Evaluating the first of these integrals, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{-3|x|+2} & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{3x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}{e}^{3x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3x+2}\,{|}_{a}^{0}\,) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{3}{e}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3a+2}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}-0 \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand ${e}^{-3|x|+2}$ is an **even** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-3|x|+2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }{e}^{-3|x|+2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{-3|x|+2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-3|x|+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{3}+\frac{{e}^{2}}{3} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
